title: Animals Thought Extinct Found Alive (One Was Hiding on a Rock for 80 Years)
title_candidates: Animals Thought Extinct Found Alive (One Was Hiding on a Rock for 80 Years)
Animals Scientists Thought Were Extinct (But Then Found Alive)
Extinct Animals Found Alive: The Fish Older Than Dinosaurs
blurb:
Can an animal really come back from extinction? These did. A fish that was supposed to have died with the dinosaurs, a coelacanth found at a fish market on a honeymoon, a bird that hid for 50 years, a ferret rediscovered by a ranch dog named Shep, and a giant insect hiding on a sea cliff for 80 years. Meatball tells the whole story.

Which extinct animal would you bring back? Best answer gets read out next time 👇

beats.say: This insect was declared extinct. Rats ate every last one on its island. Eighty years later, it turned up alive, on a rock in the middle of the ocean. That story's at the end. You will not love its face.
This fish was supposed to have died out with the dinosaurs. A fishing boat pulled one up anyway.
This bird vanished for fifty years.
And this ferret came back from extinction because a farm dog called Shep brought one home.
I'm Meatball. I narrate nature. Nature, frankly, keeps trying to eat me. Today: animals scientists thought were extinct, and how every one of them was found alive.
This fish died out with the dinosaurs. At least, that's what every scientist on Earth thought, until 1938.
beats.loop_say: I'm not saying textbooks are wrong. I'm just saying,
beats.short_title: The Fish That Was 'Extinct' for 66 Million Years 🐟
beats.bonus: Its genus, Latimeria, is named after the museum curator who spotted it.

beats.say: It's called a coelacanth. Scientists only knew it from fossils like this one. Very flat. Not much of a swimmer.
Then, in South Africa, a museum curator named Marjorie Courtenay-Latimer checked a fishing boat's catch and found a big blue fish with fins like little legs.
A fish expert, James Smith, saw her sketch and confirmed it. A living coelacanth. Sixty six million years of being extinct, and it was just in the ocean, being a fish.
Not extinct. Just busy.
Quick thing. If watching a meatball narrate things that might eat him is your idea of fun, subscribing genuinely keeps me off the menu. That's how it works. I checked.
And it's a weird fish. It can grow as long as a grown-up person. Scientists now think coelacanths can live for about a hundred years, and may stay pregnant for five.
Five years. Somewhere out there is a fish who has been expecting since before you got your phone.
A biologist found a brand new species of coelacanth on his honeymoon. At a fish market. For sale.
beats.loop_say: Most people bring home a fridge magnet. Meanwhile,
beats.short_title: He Found a 'Dinosaur Fish' on His Honeymoon 🐟
beats.bonus: A second Indonesian coelacanth was caught by local fishermen in July 1998.
beats.comment: What's the weirdest thing you've brought home from a trip? 👇 Follow Meatball for more 🍝

beats.say: It was 1997, in Indonesia. Mark Erdmann and his wife Arnaz were walking through a market when she noticed a strange, big fish on a cart.
He knew that face right away. It was a coelacanth, on the far side of the Indian Ocean from the first ones. Scientists later named it a separate species.
For the record, it was at a market. For sale. To eat. I would like everyone to sit with that.
beats.aside: (a fish market is not a museum)

beats.say: This bird was declared extinct in 1898. Fifty years later, a doctor followed some footprints up a mountain in New Zealand, and found it.
beats.loop_say: Always check the tall grass. Because
beats.bonus: Today there are around 500 takahē, and the number is slowly growing.
beats.comment: Would you have kept looking? 👇 Follow Meatball for more 🍝

beats.say: His name was Geoffrey Orbell. He'd seen tracks like these, and he would not let it go.
In November 1948, in the Murchison Mountains, there they were. Takahē. A giant flightless swamphen with a beak like a pair of red garden shears.
It mostly eats grass. Just grass. All day. Honestly, my favourite animal in this whole video.
Here's the sad twist. The last takahē anyone saw before it vanished, back in 1898, was caught by a dog.
Dogs, one. Takahē, zero. Remember that score. It changes in a minute.
Today there are around five hundred takahē, and the number is slowly going up. Slowly. They're not in a rush. They eat grass.
This ferret was declared extinct in 1979. Two years later, a ranch dog in Wyoming named Shep brought one home.
beats.loop_say: Give that dog a medal. Because
beats.bonus: Biologists then found a colony of more than 100 black-footed ferrets near Meeteetse, Wyoming.
beats.comment: What's the weirdest thing your dog has brought home? 👇 Follow Meatball for more 🍝

beats.say: Shep's family didn't know what it was. A taxidermist did, and called wildlife officials.
Biologists searched the area and found a whole colony. More than a hundred black-footed ferrets, hiding in prairie dog towns.
So that's dogs back level. Shep found an endangered species. Most dogs find a sock.
Shep deserves a medal. I can't afford one. But if you hit like, I'll tell him it's from you.
Now. What do black-footed ferrets eat? Prairie dogs. Up to ninety percent of their diet. A mother with babies can get through hundreds of them a year.
Hundreds. Of something roughly my size. I'd like a short break.
Then it went wrong. Disease tore through the colony. Between 1985 and 1987, biologists caught the last eighteen and moved them to safety.
It worked. Ferrets bred in captivity have been released across the American West, and a few hundred live wild today. One was even cloned, in 2020, from cells frozen back in the 1980s.
Frozen in the eighties. Back in 2020. Which is, coincidentally, how I feel about leftovers.
This insect was declared extinct after rats took over its island. Eighty years later, scientists found it clinging to a sea cliff, under one single bush.
beats.loop_say: I'm not saying climb a cliff at night. I'm just saying,
beats.short_title: This Insect Hid on a Rock for 80 Years 🪲
beats.bonus: The rock is Ball's Pyramid, about 23 km from Lord Howe Island, Australia.
beats.comment: Would you climb it at night? 👇 Follow Meatball for more 🍝

beats.say: The cliff is Ball's Pyramid. A spike of rock over five hundred metres tall, sticking out of the ocean near Lord Howe Island, Australia.
In 2001, two scientists, David Priddel and Nicholas Carlile, searched it. Under one bush, they found droppings. So they came back after dark, with flashlights.
And there they were. Twenty four Lord Howe Island stick insects. Each one about as long as your hand. Shiny, black, and known locally as the tree lobster.
I promised you the face. There it is. The tree lobster. Finally, something with lobster in its name, and nobody's looking at me.
How did it end up there? Nobody knows for sure. What we do know: in 1918, a supply ship ran aground on Lord Howe Island. Black rats got ashore. Within a couple of years, the stick insects were gone.
Rats. On an island. Eating everything in sight. I need everyone to stay calm.
In 2003, scientists took two pairs off the rock. One pair went to Melbourne Zoo, where keepers named them Adam and Eve. Almost every tree lobster at the zoo comes from that one pair.
beats.loop_say: Two bugs. Thousands of babies. And it all started when
beats.short_title: One Pair of Bugs Saved a Whole Species 🪲
beats.bonus: Zoos in Europe and North America now breed them too.
beats.comment: What would you have named them? 👇 Follow Meatball for more 🍝

beats.say: It nearly failed. Eve got sick, and keepers nursed her back. Since then the zoo has hatched thousands of eggs, and other zoos around the world have joined in.
One pair. Thousands of bugs.
And the ending? A huge rat removal project began on Lord Howe Island in 2019. The plan is to bring the tree lobster home one day, after more than a hundred years away.
So that's the file. A fish, a bird, a ferret and an insect. All declared extinct. All found alive. By a curator, a doctor, a dog, and two people with flashlights.
The lesson? Sometimes extinct just means nobody looked in the right place yet. Though for most extinct animals, sadly, gone really does mean gone.
